## Management of the Chinese muntjac {#sec-management}

The Invasive Alien Species Regulation stipulates that the Chinese muntjac must be managed aiming at (rapid) eradication where possible, and control or containment otherwise (see @sec-legislation).
In Flanders, management of the species primarily consists of **targeted removal through hunting**. 
Action can be initiated through a rapid response protocol:
when a new sighting is reported and verified, a hunter is mobilized as quickly as possible to attempt removal.
Alternatively, in areas where the species has established, dedicated campaigns are organized during the winter months.
Such management efforts are carried out by ANB wildlife managers and ANB-authorized hunters, including members of the Hubertus-vereniging (@sec-cousers).

Two principal eradication or control methods have been used in Flanders: blind and stalk hunting.
**Blind hunting**, or hunting from a blind, involves positioning a hunter at a fixed vantage point, a hunting blind, and waiting for an animal to pass by.
In contrast, **stalk hunting**, or stalking, involves hunters actively and attentively moving through the habitat in search of animals.
Blind hunting has been used in the past, but remained rather ineffective: due to the species’ small size, crepuscular activity, and preference for dense understory cover, detection and shooting opportunities are generally rare and require long, unproductive waiting periods.
Nowadays, the more effective, but also more risky, stalking is the preferred method.
It increases encounter rates and allows hunters to scan undergrowth more thoroughly, particularly in winter when vegetation is sparse.
Other management techniques involve trapping or netting, for a detailed discussion see @casaer_best_2015.

Although complete eradication of the Chinese muntjac in Flanders has proven difficult, some **successes have been recorded** [cf. @dhondt_monitoring_2023].
Between January 2019 and July 2023, 53 animals have officially been reported to ANB as removed, most of them in the core distribution area east of Antwerp city (@sec-invasions).
On the other hand, numbers of sightings have repeatedly recovered rather quickly following control-correlated reductions.
This might point to successful reproduction and/or immigration of animals from surrounding areas (i.e., source-sink dynamic, see @sec-biology).
In addition also emigration of animals into surrounding areas can be triggered by management activities.
